modules.title: Special gifts and gratitude
modules.outcome: say thank you and name things we are grateful for
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Special gifts and gratitude', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: say thank you and name things we are grateful for. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen and talk: hear a short story, text or example linked to 'Special gifts and gratitude' and say what it means in your own words.
Connect: name one place in your own day where it applies.
Use it: say thank you and name things we are grateful for. Practise with care and respect, in class and at home.
Reflect: what went well, what was hard, and one thing you will do next time.
modules.example: Solved: Empathy steps: notice, ask, listen, say back what you heard, offer help. After a mistake: what happened, what I learned, what I will do next. Method: Model run for 'Special gifts and gratitude'. A short text or story is read aloud. Learners say the main lesson in one sentence. In pairs they find one moment in school or home where this lesson would help. Each learner plans one small action for the week and tells it to a partner. At the end of the week they report back. What a good answer looks like: the lesson is in the learner's own words, the example is real and local, and the action is small enough to do. Content follows the approved local syllabus and is checked by a qualified teacher.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Say thank you and name things we are grateful for: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Learn that gifts are not only things. A gift can be a toy, but also a kind friend, a good meal, a clean park, or a talent like singing. Draw one gift you have that is not something you bought.
Step 2, Learn what gratitude means. Gratitude is feeling thankful and showing it. When someone gives you a gift or helps you, you can say, 'Thank you for helping me.' Say it with eyes up and a smile.

Step 3, Practise thank-you sentences with a reason. 'Thank you, Grandma, for cooking dinner.' 'Thank you, teacher, for helping me read.' Adding the reason shows you noticed what the person did, and that makes the thanks feel real.

Step 4, Make a gratitude list. Name three things you are grateful for today: for example my family, clean water and my friend. If you list 3 things a day for 5 days, you will have 15 things. Write or draw them.

Step 5, Notice how it feels. When you say thank you, the other person feels happy and so do you. Gratitude can turn a bad day around because it helps you look at what is good, not only what is missing.

Step 6, Your turn: write one thank-you sentence to a person who helped you this week and name two things you are grateful for. Answer: 'Thank you, Dad, for helping with my bag.' I am grateful for my friends and my home.

modules.title: Friendship
modules.outcome: solve a small friendship problem kindly
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Friendship', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: solve a small friendship problem kindly. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen and talk: hear a short story, text or example linked to 'Friendship' and say what it means in your own words.
Connect: name one place in your own day where it applies.
Use it: solve a small friendship problem kindly. Practise with care and respect, in class and at home.
Reflect: what went well, what was hard, and one thing you will do next time.
modules.example: Solved: A friend says 'skip class'. Steps: stay calm, say no clearly, offer another plan, walk away, tell a trusted adult if it continues. Method: Model run for 'Friendship'. A short text or story is read aloud. Learners say the main lesson in one sentence. In pairs they find one moment in school or home where this lesson would help. Each learner plans one small action for the week and tells it to a partner. At the end of the week they report back. What a good answer looks like: the lesson is in the learner's own words, the example is real and local, and the action is small enough to do. Content follows the approved local syllabus and is checked by a qualified teacher.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Solve a small friendship problem kindly: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, The problem: Laila and Dana are friends. At playtime both want the same red scooter. Laila grabs it first, Dana frowns and says, 'You always get it,' and walks away looking upset.

Step 2, Name the feelings: Laila notices Dana is sad and a little cross. Laila feels bad too, because she wants her friend. Naming feelings, 'I am sad, she is cross,' helps both children calm down before talking.
Step 3, Choices: Laila could ride away and ignore Dana, say 'It is mine,' or fix the problem. She thinks of two kind fixes, taking turns or finding another game they can do together.
Step 4, Kind words: Laila walks over and says, 'Sorry I grabbed it. Let's take turns. I go to the wall, then you go.' Her words say sorry, give an idea, and use a calm voice with no shouting.
Step 5, Result: Dana says, 'Okay, you first, then me.' Laila rides to the wall and back, gives Dana the scooter, and Dana rides. Both children had a turn, and the friendship is safe.
Step 6, Why it worked: Laila said sorry, used a fair idea, and listened. A small problem does not need to end a friendship if each child shows care. Friends solve problems kindly, not by winning.

Your turn: Two friends both want the last green crayon. What should they do and say? Model answer: one says, 'Can we take turns? You use it first for two minutes, then I do.' Both agree, share the crayon kindly, and stay friends.

modules.title: Responsibility
modules.outcome: keep a simple class or home job
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Responsibility', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: keep a simple class or home job. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.

modules.example: Solved: Class jobs: Monday Asha waters plants, Tuesday Ben tidies books. A fair rule: everyone takes a turn, and everyone knows it in advance. Method: Model run for 'Responsibility'. A short text or story is read aloud. Learners say the main lesson in one sentence. In pairs they find one moment in school or home where this lesson would help. Each learner plans one small action for the week and tells it to a partner. At the end of the week they report back. What a good answer looks like: the lesson is in the learner's own words, the example is real and local, and the action is small enough to do. Content follows the approved local syllabus and is checked by a qualified teacher.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Keep a simple class or home job: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, The job: Karim agrees to be the plant helper for his class. His job is to water the two class plants every Monday and Thursday before the first lesson. Having a clear job with clear days makes it simple.
Step 2, Make a reminder: Karim draws a small chart with two rows, Monday and Thursday, and a tick box beside each. He puts the chart near the door where he can see it as he comes in each morning.
Step 3, Do the job: On Monday he fills the small jug with water, gives each plant one jug, wipes a drop from the table, and ticks the Monday box. The plants are watered and the table is clean.
Step 4, A hard day: On Thursday Karim forgets until lunch. He does not hide it. He tells his teacher, 'I forgot the plants.' He waters them straight away and ticks the box with a note, 'late'.

Step 5, Why honesty matters: Being responsible does not mean never forgetting. It means doing what you promised, owning a mistake, and fixing it quickly. The plants are fine, and his teacher trusts him because he told the truth.
Step 6, Count the result: In one week Karim did 2 of 2 jobs, one on time and one late. Next week he moves the chart to his bag so he sees it on both days. Fixing the system helps him remember.

Your turn: You must feed the home pet every evening. Make a plan for one week and say what to do if you forget. Model answer: tick chart on the fridge, feed at 6 pm, and if you forget, tell an adult at once and feed it now.

modules.title: Fairness and rules
modules.outcome: take turns and explain why rules help
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Fairness and rules', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: take turns and explain why rules help. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.

modules.example: Solved: Class jobs: Monday Asha waters plants, Tuesday Ben tidies books. A fair rule: everyone takes a turn, and everyone knows it in advance. Method: Model run for 'Fairness and rules'. A short text or story is read aloud. Learners say the main lesson in one sentence. In pairs they find one moment in school or home where this lesson would help. Each learner plans one small action for the week and tells it to a partner. At the end of the week they report back. What a good answer looks like: the lesson is in the learner's own words, the example is real and local, and the action is small enough to do. modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Take turns and explain why rules help: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, The game: Four children, Bilal, Aisha, Sami and Rana, want to use one slide at the same time in the playground. Everybody pushes toward the ladder, and Sami almost falls.
Step 2, What goes wrong: With no rule, the biggest or fastest child wins and the others get hurt or left out. Aisha says, 'This is not fair and it is not safe.' The children agree they need a rule.

Step 3, Make a rule: Rana suggests, 'We line up in a row, and each person goes down once, then goes to the back.' The line gives the order: Bilal, Aisha, Sami, Rana. Everyone understands who goes next.
Step 4, Take turns: Bilal slides first and walks to the back. Aisha goes second, Sami third, Rana fourth. After four slides each child has had exactly one turn, so the count is equal at one each.

Step 5, A child breaks the rule: Sami tries to go twice in a row. Aisha says calmly, 'It is Rana's turn, then you.' Sami goes to the back and waits. The rule is the same for every child, so it is fair.

Step 6, Explain it: Rules help because they keep us safe, give everyone a turn and stop arguments. The slide rule works for the big child and the small child in the same way, and that is what fairness means.

Your turn: Three children share two scooters at break. Make a fair rule. Model answer: two ride for three minutes while one waits, then the waiting child swaps with one rider. Over three turns each child rides twice and waits once.
